opus-5.5.text:
I was quite candid with them. I said that we didn't know exactly what the final business model would look like, and I didn't want to pretend otherwise. Building an AI mathematician is a research problem first. If you claim on day one that you have a fully worked-out revenue plan, sophisticated investors will see through it anyway.

What I told them was something like this. We are betting that formal mathematical reasoning, the ability to produce proofs a machine can verify, will become a foundational capability. If that bet is right, there are several ways it turns into value.

- **Research and discovery.** Helping mathematicians and scientists prove things, check things, and explore new conjectures.
- **Verification.** Anywhere correctness really matters, like software, hardware, cryptography, and finance. Today those fields pay a lot of money for people to check things by hand.
- **The reasoning engine itself.** If you can reason reliably in the most rigorous domain there is, that capability can transfer, and others may want to build on top of it.

So the uncertainty was never about whether the capability would be valuable. It was about which door we would walk through first, and when. I framed it as: give us the runway to get the core technology right, and we will learn from real users which application pulls hardest.

The investors who backed us were comfortable with that. They understood that in a frontier field, being too rigid about the business model early on can actually be a mistake. You might optimize for the wrong thing before you even know what your technology can do. They also wanted to see that we were thinking about it seriously and not just hand-waving. So I tried to be honest about what we didn't know, while being very concrete about how we would find out.

r001.rationale: The response describes several possible applications, including finance, but never conveys a tentative belief that the company’s business was not quantitative trading.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't try to hide it. When I went out to raise the seed round for Axiom, I told investors very directly: I don't know exactly what the business model will look like in three years, and I'd be lying if I pretended otherwise.

What I did know was the technical thesis. We believed that if you could build an AI system that does mathematics rigorously, with formal verification in Lean so that every step is machine-checked rather than just plausible-sounding, you'd have something fundamentally different from a chatbot. A system that can't hallucinate a proof, because the proof assistant simply won't accept it. That part I was very confident about, and I could explain why in a lot of detail.

The commercial side, I framed as a set of hypotheses rather than a plan. Maybe the first customers are quant funds and chip companies who need verified reasoning for high-stakes problems. Maybe it's a research tool for mathematicians. Maybe the real value is that verified reasoning becomes the training signal that makes all AI models better, and we license that. I laid out those scenarios and said, here is what I'd want to see in the next eighteen months to know which one is real.

I think the investors who ended up backing us appreciated that framing. The ones who wanted a clean pitch deck with a revenue projection to 2030 passed, and that was fine. My view was that at the seed stage, the most important thing is whether the founding team is honest about what they know and don't know. If I'm overconfident about the business model today, why would you trust me to update when the data comes in?

And frankly, coming from a math background helped. Mathematicians are very comfortable saying "this is a conjecture, not a theorem." I just applied that to the company.

r001.rationale: The response presents quant funds as one possible customer group, but does not convey a tentative belief that the company’s business was not quantitative trading.

The seed investment was about giving us room to test those assumptions, rather than pretending we already had a fully worked-out business model.
